subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Price Anchoring in Menus
description: A fast breakdown of Price Anchoring in Menus for builders.

hook.text: A $150 steak sits at the top of the menu. Nobody orders it. But the $65 steak now looks reasonable by comparison.

buildup.text: Restaurants place expensive items first to anchor your perception of value. Everything below feels like a deal.

discovery.text: The anchor sets the range. Without the $150 item, the $65 steak feels expensive. With it, it feels moderate.

twist.text: Removing dollar signs from menus increases spending by about 8%. The symbol $30 triggers pain of paying.

climax.text: Every price you see on a menu is positioned to guide your choice. The format, placement, and neighbors all influence.

punchline.text: The most expensive item sells the second most expensive.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a $150 steak on a restaurant menu?
options: To sell that specific steak to high-end customers
To make other expensive items seem more reasonable by comparison
To demonstrate the quality of the restaurant

details.summary: Menu anchoring places expensive items prominently to make other items seem reasonably priced by comparison. The anchor shifts perception of value so that a forty-dollar steak seems reasonable next to a hundred-dollar bottle of wine.
details.whyItMatters: Restaurant and retail menus are carefully engineered psychological documents. Anchor items are often not meant to sell but to make target items seem like good value.
takeaways: Expensive anchor items make other items seem like better value
Anchor items often exist primarily to shift perception, not to sell
Menu design influences which items customers choose and how much they spend

faq.question: How does menu anchoring actually work?
faq.answer: By placing a very expensive item first, every subsequent price is evaluated against that anchor. A thirty-dollar entree that might seem expensive on its own feels moderate compared to a sixty-dollar entree shown just above it.

faq.question: Do luxury restaurants use anchoring differently than fast food?
faq.answer: Yes. Luxury menus remove dollar signs, avoid price columns, and embed prices within descriptions to reduce price salience. Fast food menus highlight value meals and combos that anchor against individual item prices.
